blocks.instruction: Leia o texto e escolha a alternativa correta. Algumas perguntas pedem inferência — a resposta não está escrita com todas as letras.
blocks.passage:
Ethical reputation is unusual as a business asset: it takes decades to build, and weeks, sometimes days, to destroy. Few companies ever fully recover from a serious reputational episode, and even those that do rarely return to quite the same trust they held before. That asymmetry — slow to earn, fast to lose — has profound implications for how senior leaders make decisions on the edges of what is merely legal.

Short-term pressures will always exist. There will always be a quarter in which a difficult compromise would make the numbers look better, and the consequences feel distant. The leaders who build long-lived companies tend to be the ones who, quietly, declined those compromises long before the public spotlight could ever have noticed. They did so not from saintliness but from a clear-eyed understanding of the arithmetic: reputational capital, once burned, is almost never fully restored.

There is also a subtler point about institutional culture. Each time senior leaders decline a questionable shortcut — and, equally, each time they fail to decline one — they are quietly teaching the organisation what is acceptable. Those lessons, accumulated over years, become the unwritten standards by which thousands of decisions are taken at the edges of the business. Reputation is thus less a public relations exercise than a quiet, continuous exercise in institutional self-authorship.

items.q: What is the "asymmetry" the text describes?
options: Large firms recover faster than small ones
Legal risk is higher than ethical risk
Reputation is slow to earn but fast to lose
Short-term profit outweighs long-term cost
items.why: "slow to earn, fast to lose" — décadas para construir, semanas para destruir.

items.q: According to the text, why did the best leaders decline questionable compromises?
options: Because regulators were watching closely
From a clear-eyed understanding of the arithmetic
Out of pure moral saintliness
To impress the public and the press
items.why: "not from saintliness but from a clear-eyed understanding of the arithmetic."

items.q: What does the text say each declined shortcut teaches?
options: The organisation what is acceptable
Competitors what the firm will not do
The board how to cut costs
Nothing beyond the immediate decision
items.why: "they are quietly teaching the organisation what is acceptable."

items.q: Which statement would the author most likely DISAGREE with?
options: A single episode can undo decades of trust
Culture is shaped by accumulated small decisions
Reputation is largely a public relations exercise
Integrity often has to be chosen when no one is watching
items.why: Inferência: o texto define reputação como algo mais profundo que RP — 'institutional self-authorship'.

items.q: The phrase "far from the executive floor" suggests that…
options: distance from the CEO reduces ethical risk
front-line decisions are guided by standards leaders set indirectly
most ethical failures happen at headquarters
senior leaders approve every decision personally
items.why: Inferência: o tom da liderança vira o padrão pelo qual milhares de decisões distantes são tomadas.

blocks.instruction: Ouça Charlotte encerrar o fórum interno de ética. Responda sem ler a transcrição — ela só aparece depois de corrigir.

audio.text:
I want to close by putting a number on the wall that isn't in any of your slides: one hundred and sixty years. That is how long this company has been trading. Almost none of us in this room will still be here for the next sixty. And yet the decisions we take this year will quietly shape the standards someone inherits long after we've gone.

I've sat in enough of these forums to be wary of grand statements about values. So let me be practical. The dangerous decisions are almost never the obviously wrong ones — those are easy to refuse. They are the small compromises in a difficult quarter, the shortcut that no one outside would ever notice. Take one, and you haven't just moved a number; you've set a quiet precedent for everyone below you.

What I'd ask you to hold on to is this. Reputational capital, once it's burned, is almost never fully restored. So when the pressure comes — and it will — the question is not whether we are clever enough to get away with it. The question is what kind of company we are willing to hand over. That, and nothing grander, is stewardship.
audio.label: Ouça quantas vezes precisar. A transcrição aparece depois de corrigir.

items.q: Why does Charlotte put "one hundred and sixty years" on the wall?
options: To compare Czarnikow with older rivals
To celebrate a record quarter
To announce a new anniversary campaign
To frame decisions across generations of the company
items.why: Ela usa os 160 anos para situar as decisões de hoje numa história longa que outros herdarão.

items.q: Which decisions does Charlotte call the dangerous ones?
options: The obviously illegal ones
The ones the board reviews
The ones taken by junior staff
The small compromises no one outside would notice
items.why: "the small compromises in a difficult quarter, the shortcut that no one outside would ever notice."

items.q: What does Charlotte say happens when you take such a shortcut?
options: You lose the trust of one client only
You must report it to the regulator
You set a quiet precedent for everyone below you
You save the quarter with no lasting effect
items.why: "you've set a quiet precedent for everyone below you."

items.q: When Charlotte says the question is "what kind of company we are willing to hand over," she implies that…
options: leadership should focus on this year's numbers
the company will soon be sold
ethics should be judged by what survives you, not by getting away with it
cleverness is the main test of a good executive
items.why: Inferência: ela contrasta 'ser esperto o bastante para escapar' com o que se deixa como herança.

items.q: How would you best describe Charlotte's stance on "grand statements about values"?
options: She embraces them enthusiastically
She is wary of them and prefers something practical
She dismisses ethics as PR
She thinks values cannot be discussed at all
items.why: Inferência: "wary of grand statements about values… let me be practical."

blocks.instruction: O vocabulário da lição aparece aqui em frases novas. Escolha o sentido ou a palavra que cabe no contexto.

items.q: "Twenty years of goodwill was reputational capital the firm spent in a single week." Reputational capital is…
options: the accumulated trust a company can draw on
the legal budget for litigation
the marketing spend on brand campaigns
the cash reserves held for a crisis
items.why: Capital reputacional = a confiança acumulada, um ativo que se gasta e raramente se recompõe.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "Ethics is defined by a stark ___: reputation is slow to earn and fast to lose."
options: hierarchy
consensus
symmetry
asymmetry
items.why: Asymmetry = assimetria: o desequilíbrio entre construir e destruir.

items.q: "Approving that expense report set a quiet precedent the whole desk soon followed." A quiet precedent is…
options: a public announcement of standards
an unspoken example that others copy
a one-off exception with no effect
a formal written policy
items.why: Precedente silencioso = um exemplo não declarado que passa a orientar o comportamento dos demais.

items.q: Tone at the top is best described as…
options: the CEO's speaking style in public
the seniority of the board members
the leadership's example that shapes the culture below
the volume of internal communications
items.why: Tone at the top = o exemplo dado pela liderança, que se torna cultura na base.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "Guiding an institution across generations is a form of ___ — a duty of care, not ownership."
options: arbitrage
governance audit
leverage
stewardship
items.why: Stewardship = zelo / custódia: cuidar de algo em nome de quem virá depois.

blocks.instruction: Expressões que aparecem em conversas de ética e reputação corporativa. Escolha o sentido no contexto.

items.q: "We refused to cut corners on the audit, even under deadline pressure." To cut corners means to…
options: delegate the task to juniors
reduce the size of the team
escalate the issue to the board
do something the cheap or improper way to save time
items.why: Cut corners = economizar de forma imprópria, sacrificando qualidade ou integridade.

items.q: "The board decided to hold the line on the ethics policy despite the lost deal." To hold the line means to…
options: wait for further instructions
quietly change the policy
put the decision on hold
refuse to lower a standard under pressure
items.why: Hold the line = manter a posição, não ceder ao apesar da pressão.

items.q: "One scandal and years of trust can go up in smoke." This means the trust will…
options: be destroyed suddenly and completely
be rebuilt within a quarter
be quietly transferred to a rival
become harder to measure
items.why: Go up in smoke = desaparecer de forma súbita e total.

items.q: "If we take that shortcut, it will come back to haunt us." This means it will…
options: reassure our investors
be forgotten quickly
improve this quarter's numbers
cause problems for us later
items.why: Come back to haunt us = voltar a nos prejudicar mais tarde.

items.q: "Leadership has to walk the talk, not just publish a code of conduct." To walk the talk means to…
options: delegate ethics to compliance
act in line with what you claim to value
circulate the message widely
explain the policy clearly
items.why: Walk the talk = agir de acordo com o que se prega, dar o exemplo na prática.
